studies.name: IPCC AR6 WGIII Chapter 12: Cross-sectoral Perspectives (Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change)
studies.draft_uses: April 2022 final government distribution / July 2023 Cambridge University Press online publication — CDR definitions, roles of CDR in mitigation pathways, IEA Net Zero scenario DACCS figure of 0.6 GtCO2 in 2050, CDR method maturity and potential ranges, national CDR policy landscape
studies.latest_known: July 2023 Cambridge University Press publication (identical content to April 2022 IPCC release). No update or erratum issued. AR7 not expected until ~2028. However, the draft quotes the IEA Net Zero scenario as deploying DACCS at '0.6 GtCO2 in 2050'; multiple IEA and third-party sources consistently report the IEA NZE DAC figure as ~980 MtCO2 (~0.98 GtCO2) in 2050, not 0.6 GtCO2. This figure-level discrepancy requires verification against the exact passage in Ch.12 — it may reflect a different IEA scenario vintage or a transcription error in the draft.
studies.what_changed: The specific figure '0.6 GtCO2' for IEA NZE DACCS in 2050 does not match the IEA's own published NZE figure of ~0.98 GtCO2 (~980 MtCO2) for DAC in 2050. Whether this is a Ch.12 figure or a draft transcription error cannot be resolved without re-reading Ch.12, but the IEA NZE scenario itself has been updated in subsequent IEA World Energy Outlook editions (2022, 2023, 2024, 2025) and the 0.6 figure is not corroborated by any current IEA source found.

studies.name: Lamb WF et al. 'The carbon dioxide removal gap' — Nature Climate Change
studies.draft_uses: Described in the sources list as published in '2023'; used for: (a) the statement that rapid emissions reductions are the dominant mitigation source while CDR has an important role; (b) identification of a 'CDR gap' between national proposals and IAM scenarios for 1.5°C; (c) finding that the most ambitious national proposals are close to a low-energy-demand scenario; (d) observation that many countries propose land-based removals but none commit to scaling novel methods
studies.latest_known: The paper was published 3 May 2024 (online) / June 2024 (issue) in Nature Climate Change vol. 14, pp. 644–651 — not 2023 as the draft states. A follow-up commentary by Lamb et al. ('Countries need to provide clarity on the role of carbon dioxide removal in their climate pledges') appeared in Environmental Research Letters in November 2024. The State of CDR 3rd Edition (June 2026), co-led by Lamb, contains a dedicated CDR gap chapter (Chapter 9) that updates the gap analysis using NDCs submitted through September 2025 and finds the 2030 CDR gap is 0.3 GtCO2/yr against a median Paris-compatible scenario level of 2.9 GtCO2/yr, and that the gap is 'large and growing' toward 2050.
studies.what_changed: 1. The draft's source list gives the year as '2023'; the correct publication year is 2024. 2. The CDR gap analysis has been updated in the State of CDR 3rd Edition (June 2026, Chapter 9): the 2030 gap is now quantified at 0.3 GtCO2/yr (country pledges reach 2.5 GtCO2/yr vs. a scenario median of 2.9 GtCO2/yr), and the gap is described as 'large and growing' toward 2050. The draft's qualitative conclusions (gap exists; most ambitious proposals close to low-demand scenario; no novel method commitments) remain directionally consistent with the 2026 update, but the specific gap figures and the country-level picture have changed materially, including the impact of the US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement in January 2026.

studies.name: Minx JC et al. 'Negative emissions—Part 1: Research landscape and synthesis' — Environmental Research Letters 13 (2018) 063001
studies.draft_uses: 2018 publication — used for: definition of negative emissions as intentional human efforts (not natural sinks); finding that large-scale deployment of NETs is a bio-physical requirement for 1.5°C; description of NETs as 'almost indispensable' for Paris goals; finding that NETs in cost-optimising scenarios impede early emissions reductions; caution that no single technology can sustainably meet 1.5°C pathway demands; suggestion that portfolios of methods at modest scales could be invaluable
studies.latest_known: The 2018 paper has not been retracted or formally superseded by a direct replacement article. However, the IPCC AR6 WGIII (2022) and the State of CDR 3rd Edition (June 2026, Edwards et al., doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/ZRD65) now constitute the authoritative updated synthesis of the same research landscape. No newer version of the Minx et al. Part 1 paper itself has been published. The qualitative conclusions the draft draws from it are broadly consistent with the 2022 and 2026 assessments, but the 2018 paper's scenario base is now eight years old.
studies.what_changed: Cannot positively confirm the 2018 paper's specific figures and scenario characterisations remain the latest available. The State of CDR 3rd Edition (2026) provides a comprehensive updated assessment of CDR costs, potentials, and the research landscape that covers the same ground with data through 2025. The draft's qualitative claims drawn from Minx et al. (moral hazard, portfolio approach, no single technology sufficient) are directionally consistent with later literature, but the underlying scenario evidence base has been substantially updated by AR6 (2022) and the State of CDR 3rd Edition (2026).

studies.name: Fuss S et al. 'Negative emissions—Part 2: Costs, potentials and side effects' — Environmental Research Letters 13 (2018) 063002
studies.draft_uses: 2018 publication — used for: best-estimate sustainable global potentials in 2050 (afforestation/reforestation 0.5–3.6 GtCO2/yr; BECCS 0.5–5; biochar 0.5–2; enhanced weathering 2–4; DACCS 0.5–5; soil carbon up to 5); 1.5°C pathways reaching net zero CO2 between 2046–2056 (15th–85th percentiles); net negative emissions of 1.3–29 GtCO2/yr in second half of century; removal deployment of 5–15 GtCO2/yr by 2050 in most scenarios; concern that 10–20 GtCO2/yr via BECCS is not possible without severe adverse side effects; policy conclusion to limit dependence on NETs and not delay emissions peak
studies.latest_known: The State of CDR 3rd Edition (June 2026, Edwards et al., doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/ZRD65) contains a dedicated Chapter 10 on costs and potentials that provides updated estimates for all major CDR methods using literature through 2025. The IPCC AR6 WGIII Chapter 12 (2022) also updated the potential ranges. The 2018 Fuss et al. figures are now eight years old and have been substantially revised in subsequent assessments — for example, the State of CDR 3rd Edition reports novel CDR currently at ~0.002 GtCO2/yr growing at ~40% annually, and updated cost and potential ranges differ from the 2018 estimates across multiple methods.
studies.what_changed: The specific potential ranges the draft quotes from Fuss et al. 2018 (e.g., DACCS 0.5–5 GtCO2/yr, enhanced weathering 2–4, BECCS 0.5–5, soil carbon up to 5, biochar 0.5–2, afforestation/reforestation 0.5–3.6) have been updated in the State of CDR 3rd Edition (2026) Chapter 10 and in IPCC AR6 WGIII Ch.12 (2022). The 2018 scenario characterisations (net zero CO2 between 2046–2056; net negative 1.3–29 GtCO2/yr; 5–15 GtCO2/yr by 2050) are drawn from pre-AR6 scenario literature and have been superseded by the AR6 scenario ensemble. The draft presents these 2018 figures as current best estimates without noting they predate the AR6 assessment by four years and the State of CDR 3rd Edition by eight years.
